findings.matters: A £625,000 gap in children's savings, with the replacement sourced from a different saving line, is a reallocation a finance director would want to track at outturn.

findings.detail: The commissioning saving to keep children in or closer to Pembrokeshire in lower-cost accommodation is recorded as achieved, with Q2 savings well above the original figure.
findings.matters: Savings running well ahead of the original target in children's placements is a specific example of a council reporting progress on the cost driver that most councils are trying to move.

findings.headline: Pembrokeshire County Council says it continues to have the lowest average local authority rent in Wales
findings.detail: The paper presents this as one of its key evidence findings. It also says PCC has the lowest average rent of all social landlords operating within Pembrokeshire.
findings.matters: A low comparative rent position shapes how much headroom the council has for future increases, which other councils and lenders will want to compare.
findings.quote: PCC continues to have the lowest average local authority rent in Wales.

findings.headline: Pembrokeshire states the rent proposal is necessary to maintain HRA financial viability, meet WHQS 2023 requirements and increase affordable housing supply
findings.detail: The overall conclusion links the rent rise to HRA viability, WHQS 2023 compliance, continued investment in existing homes, decarbonisation and new affordable supply. The paper describes a moderate negative affordability impact for some tenants.
findings.matters: The council is linking a rent decision directly to HRA viability and capital programme delivery, which other councils and lenders can use as a benchmark for their own HRA positions.
findings.quote: The proposal is therefore considered necessary, proportionate and justified in order to maintain HRA financial viability

findings.headline: Approximately 57.7% of tenants receive housing cost support through Housing Benefit or Universal Credit
findings.detail: The paper cites this share of tenants as context for affordability. It states that the Housing Benefit and Universal Credit share is a mitigation route for rent increases.
findings.matters: The share of tenants whose rent is paid through benefits determines how much of any rent increase the council collects directly and how much depends on the benefits system.
findings.figures: 57.7% of tenants
findings.quote: Approximately 57.7% of tenants receive housing cost support through Housing Benefit or Universal Credit.

findings.headline: 2,187 properties remain below Pembrokeshire Standard Rent, with an estimated income loss of £671k a year
findings.detail: The paper quantifies the gap between current rents and Pembrokeshire Standard Rent as an annual income loss. The transitional increase is aimed at properties in this group.
findings.matters: A quantified annual gap between actual and standard rents is a specific income shortfall that a lender or finance officer can track against the HRA business plan.

findings.detail: The proposal would keep rents within the Welsh Government rent envelope. The paper says it also includes garage rent increases and an annual review of service charges.
findings.matters: The rent rise and the transitional top-up set the HRA's main income line for 2027-2028, and a finance director at another council can compare the structure against their own rent-setting.
findings.figures: 4.0%; up to an additional £2.55 per week
findings.quote: by 4.0% plus up to an additional £2.55 per week

findings.detail: The HMRC mileage rate increase was backdated to 6 April 2026. The council says it creates a base budget pressure for 2027-28 and that no additional funding has been received.
findings.matters: A national rate change creating an unfunded in-year pressure that carries into the next year's base budget is one a finance director at another council will also face.

findings.quote: No indication of additional funding has been received.

findings.paper_title: County Council Budget Quarter 2 Monitoring Report 2026-27
findings.headline: Housing rent arrears total £3.16m at end of Q2, with cases being selected for possession claims
findings.detail: Arrears have grown each month of 2026-27 from £2.71m in April. The report says a core group of accounts has significant arrears that continue to grow, and that notices to make a court claim for possession are being prepared.
findings.matters: Rising arrears from a core group of accounts, with possession action being started, is a housing income risk a finance director at another council will be watching.

findings.quote: Housing rent arrears to the end of Q2 total £3.16m.

findings.headline: Council Tax prior-year arrears fall from £19.479m at 31 March 2026 to £16.196m at 30 September 2026
findings.detail: The report attributes £1.8m of the reduction to arrears payments and £1.5m to a reduction in debit raised. The council also reports £1.1m of Council Tax arrears linked to self-catering properties under appeal with the Valuation Office.
findings.matters: A fall in arrears alongside a backlog of Valuation Office appeals on second-home and self-catering debt is a collection position other councils with similar premiums will recognise.
findings.figures: Prior-year arrears £19.479m (31 Mar 26) to £16.196m (30 Sept 26); payments £1.8m; debit reduction £1.5m; appeal-linked arrears £1.1m (Q1 £2.9m)
findings.quote: £1.8m of the reduction relates to payment of arrears balances

findings.paper_title: County Council Budget Quarter 2 Monitoring Report 2026-27
findings.headline: Capital expenditure is 24.15% at Q2, with the 2026-27 capital programme reduced to £176.394m from £209.549m at Q1
findings.detail: The reduction reflects £41.134k of re-phasing and re-profiling, offset by £7.979k of new capital bids. The council notes delivery remains subject to inflation, borrowing costs and nutrient neutrality requirements in the Milford Haven Waterway catchment.
findings.matters: A capital programme that has been cut by about 16% at mid-year, with the report citing nutrient neutrality as a delay risk, is a delivery pattern a finance director and a lender would both track.

findings.paper_title: County Council Budget Quarter 2 Monitoring Report 2026-27
findings.headline: Average weekly cost of an under-18 unaccompanied asylum seeker placement falls from £962 at Q1 to £632 at Q2
findings.detail: Cheaper accommodation has been procured, and new under-18 clients now cost less than the grant income received for the placement. This underspend of £0.590m partly offsets Children in Care pressures.
findings.matters: A grant-funded placement now costing less than the grant received, with the saving used to offset other children's services pressures, is a specific mechanism another council may want to compare.

findings.detail: The overspend is attributed to sustained growth in the number and complexity of clients with Learning Disabilities and Mental Health needs. Supported Accommodation is projected £0.981m over budget, and Homecare £1.350m over.
findings.matters: Growth in complex adult care packages, with the report saying the trend is expected to continue, is a demand pressure a finance director at another council will recognise.

findings.detail: Borrowing in 2025-26 was £35m against £47m assumed. A further £10m advance is projected before year end. Capital financing costs are projected £1.027m below budget, and net investment income £0.6m above budget.
findings.matters: Lower and later borrowing than planned, combined with interest on cash held before capital spend, is a position a lender and a finance director would both want to see against the original borrowing plan.

findings.detail: Usable reserves are projected to reduce from £97.3m to £69.3m during the year. The report states the reduction is mainly related to capital programme funding, including fleet purchases.
findings.matters: A drawdown of about 29% of usable reserves to fund capital is the sort of reserve use a finance director at another council will compare against their own strategy for holding reserves.

findings.headline: Projected school balances rise £1.818m to £3.364m in 2026-27 after additional Welsh Government ALN funding
findings.detail: Welsh Government confirmed an additional £60m for ALN in 2026-27, with Pembrokeshire receiving £2.112m. The council states the allocation will offset ALN costs reported at Q1, and that funding in excess of spend will increase school balances.
findings.matters: Schools moving from an in-year ALN pressure to a projected balance increase, funded by a one-year grant, shows how a specific grant can change the reserve position, and the report flags that future years are not yet confirmed.

findings.paper_title: County Council Budget Quarter 2 Monitoring Report 2026-27
findings.headline: Budget savings 83% on track at Q2, with £0.797m rated amber and £0.916m rated red against a £10.130m target
findings.detail: Of the £10.130m savings target, £8.417m is rated green. Savings not met and without an alternative are stated to add pressure to the 2026-27 budget and the MTFP, but are not yet reflected in the projected outturn.
findings.matters: A savings programme with almost a fifth of its value not yet secure, and not yet in the forecast, is the exposure a finance director would track into the next budget round.

findings.quote: with 83% being identified as on track for delivery at Quarter 2.

findings.detail: The Director of Resources contrasts the 2025-26 outturn with the 2026-27 projection. The moratorium stays in place until the projected outturn returns to a balanced budget.
findings.matters: The contrast between a prior-year underspend and a current-year overspend, with a spending freeze retained, is a pattern a finance director at another council may recognise.

findings.detail: The projected outturn is £348.6m against an approved net budget of £347.4m. The Director of Resources says the council will continue a moratorium on non-essential spending until the projected outturn returns to a balanced position.

findings.headline: Pembrokeshire's 2026-27 general capital funding set at £8.654m, up from £8.370m in 2025-26
findings.detail: The paper breaks the 2026-27 figure into £4.887m of general capital grant and £3.767m of un-hypothecated supported borrowing. It says a reduction in general capital grant would require more borrowing, and that the settlement assumption will be updated after the provisional settlement on 1 December 2026.
findings.matters: Grant levels feed straight into how much the council must borrow, so a finance director or lender would track any change to the general capital settlement.

findings.quote: For Pembrokeshire, general capital funding for 2026 -27 was set at £8.654m

findings.headline: Paper says continued increases in capital costs may create pressure to raise the 5.30% capital financing cap in future years
findings.detail: The paper calls the 5.30% cap an important safeguard for financial sustainability. It says any increase would need to be incremental and proportionate, and would need to demonstrate affordability within the longer-term strategy.
findings.matters: A council signalling that its own borrowing ceiling may move is a material change in the affordability framework lenders and peers use to judge its capacity.
findings.figures: 5.30% current cap
findings.quote: continued increases in capital costs and investment requirements may result in pressure to increase this cap in future years.

findings.headline: Cabinet lists nine potential capital projects, including Tenby Multi Storey and Milford Care Home, for consideration within borrowing capacity
findings.detail: The nine schemes are Ysgol Bro Preseli, Greenhill School, Pembrokeshire Referral Unit, Milford Haven Leisure Centre, Pembroke Leisure Centre, Milford Care Home, Fishguard Care Campus, Monkton Gypsy Traveller Site and Tenby Multi Storey. The paper says each remains subject to a business case and affordability assessment.
findings.matters: Naming specific projects against a finite borrowing envelope shows the council's priorities for new debt, which is what lenders and peers would look at when judging future pipeline demand.
findings.figures: 9 schemes listed, against £255.35m borrowing capacity
findings.quote: The inclusion of these schemes does not indicate any order of priority or commitment to proceed.

findings.headline: Pembrokeshire ranks 11th highest of 22 Welsh authorities on the capital financing costs ratio
findings.detail: The paper draws this from the Welsh Local Authorities Approved Treasury Management Strategies 2026-27. It also notes Pembrokeshire ranks 11th in Wales for scale of capital investment, 5th lowest for Council Tax, and 13th for revenue budget size.
findings.matters: A peer ranking on the same ratio gives finance officers at other Welsh councils a benchmark for their own capital affordability position.
findings.figures: 11th of 22 Welsh authorities, 5th lowest Council Tax in Wales (2026-27), 13th by revenue budget size
findings.quote: Out of the 22 local authorities in Wales, Pembrokeshire ranks as the 11th highest authority based on this measure.

findings.headline: Council says it has benefited over recent years from an underspend in budgeted capital financing costs, caused by slippage in the programme
findings.detail: The paper attributes the underspend to market capacity to deliver schemes and imprecise project profiling. Reduced capital spend meant less borrowing, letting the council use cash balances and short-term borrowing. Table 3 shows a saving of £1,027k against the 2025-26 budget.
findings.matters: A council benefiting from slippage that is now being rebased is a pattern peers see when budgeted financing costs fall short of actual, and a lender tracks it as a source of short-term cash flexibility.
findings.figures: £1,027k saving against 2025-26 budget
findings.quote: Members will recall that over the last few years the Council has benefited from an underspend in its budgeted capital financing costs.

findings.headline: General earmarked reserves used for capital shown falling from £27.8m in 2026-27 to £10.1m in 2027-28, and paper says their adequacy needs review
findings.detail: Table 6 shows General earmarked reserves funding of £27.8m in 2026-27 and £10.1m in 2027-28, then £4.1m, £6.8m and £6.4m in later years. The paper says a review of reserves is needed as costs escalate.
findings.matters: A large drawdown of earmarked reserves for capital, with a stated need to review adequacy, is the kind of reserve position finance directors and lenders track closely.
findings.quote: As costs continue to escalate there is a n ongoing need to review the adequacy of resources held within earmarked reserve

findings.headline: Prudential indicators assume £247.8m of new and replacement external borrowing between 2026-27 and 2030-31, with £55.2m of internal resources
findings.detail: The prudential indicators are based on the Table 6 programme and assume the stated borrowing and reserves draw. Table 8 shows gross external debt rising from £203.5m at 31 March 2026 to £414.8m by 2030-31, with the CFR staying above gross debt in every year.
findings.matters: Gross debt more than doubling over five years is the central exposure a lender is pricing, and the internal-resources figure shows how much of the programme relies on new borrowing.
findings.figures: £247.8m external borrowing, £55.2m internal resources, gross external debt £203.5m (2025-26 actual) to £414.8m (2030-31 estimate), CFR £292.40m to £487.20m
findings.quote: New and replacement external borrowing of £247.8m between 2026-27 and 2030-31;

findings.headline: Paper states interest rates have remained higher than assumed in the approved Treasury Management Strategy, with a 5.00% borrowing rate assumed for 2027-28
findings.detail: The paper says the target borrowing rate will need to increase, with borrowing costs expected to stay elevated in the short term before easing over the medium term. Table 1 shows 4.00% for 2026-27 and 2027-28 under the current strategy, while Table 4 assumes 5.00% for 2027-28.
findings.matters: A council revising its borrowing rate assumption upward is a direct signal of the cost of new debt, which peers and lenders use to benchmark their own financing assumptions.
findings.quote: Interest rates have remained significantly higher than assumed in the approved Treasury Management Strategy.

findings.headline: Capital financing costs ratio projected to peak at 6.46% in 2036-37 on the Table 5 borrowing requirement, above the 5.30% cap
findings.detail: The paper says the ratio rises to 5.32% in 2030-31, peaks at 6.46% in 2036-37 and falls to 5.58% by 2041-42 if the full Table 5 borrowing requirement is taken on. That is above the 5.30% cap the paper uses as its affordability test.
findings.matters: A projected breach of the council's own affordability cap, on the paper's own numbers, is what a lender or peer finance director would need to weigh when assessing long-term debt capacity.
findings.quote: Based on the borrowing requirement outlined in Table 5, the Capital Financing Costs to Net Revenue Cost ratio is projected to increase to 5.32% in 2030-31, rising to a peak of 6.46% in 2036-37

findings.headline: Paper states it will not be possible to fund all identified schemes within the 5.30% cap, and prioritisation will be required
findings.detail: The paper concludes that overall capital pressures exceed the borrowing capacity under the 5.30% cap. It says future investment decisions will need to balance service need, statutory requirements, strategic objectives and affordability.
findings.matters: This is the council stating that part of its capital pipeline is unaffordable on its own affordability framework, which bears directly on its future borrowing and on lender exposure.
findings.figures: £288m requested against £255.35m capacity
findings.quote: it will not be possible to fund all identified schemes, and a process of prioritisation will be required.

findings.headline: Directorate requests total £288m of additional PCC borrowing through 2041-42, £33m above the capacity factored into the model
findings.detail: Table 5 shows requests from Education, Social Care & Housing and Place totalling £751,853k of capital cost, of which £288,525k is PCC requirement and £463,328k external funding. The paper says the requests exceed the modelled figure by £33m.
findings.matters: Requests exceeding modelled borrowing capacity by a stated amount is a concrete gap a finance director can benchmark against their own pipeline.
findings.figures: £288m additional borrowing requested, £33m above factored-in amount, total capital cost £751,853k, PCC requirement £288,525k, external funding £463,328k
findings.quote: Over the period up to and including 2041 -42 the table shows an additional £288m borrowing could be requested, £33m more than factored in above.

findings.headline: Additional borrowing capacity under the 5.30% cap stated as £255.35m, after a £4.650m reduction for schemes approved since Quarter 2
findings.detail: Modelling gives capacity of up to £260m of additional General Fund borrowing through to 2041-42. The paper reduces this by £4.650m to £255.35m to account for schemes approved since Quarter 2 and projects whose borrowing extends beyond the MTFP.
findings.matters: The figure is the total borrowing envelope the council has set itself, so it sets the limit on new schemes that a lender or peer authority would need to know.
findings.figures: £260m modelled capacity, £4.650m reduction, £255.35m net additional borrowing capacity
findings.quote: This capacity is subsequently reduced by £4.650m to £255.35m to account for borrowing required to fund schemes approved since Quarter 2

findings.headline: Paper projects General Fund capital financing costs at 4.14% of net revenue stream in 2027-28 against a 5.30% cap
findings.detail: Table 3 shows the General Fund ratio rising from 3.65% in 2026-27 to 4.53% in 2029-30 and 4.43% in 2030-31, with capacity under the cap shrinking to 0.77% in 2029-30. The paper states the 5.30% cap is not a target.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can compare the trajectory of the ratio against their own cap, and a lender can see how much headroom remains before new borrowing breaches it.

findings.headline: Aggregate Council Tax base for 2027-28 set at 63,517.90, up from 62,581.12 for 2026-27
findings.detail: The paper attributes the increase primarily to the higher collection rate assumption, not to a change in the number of properties. Budget-purpose base rises to 57,552.85 from 57,004.49, with the second homes and long-term empty premium bases also rising.
findings.matters: The increase in the base comes from an assumption about collection rather than from new properties, so the income gain depends on that assumption holding.

findings.headline: Council Tax base for 2027-28 not adjusted for Welsh Government self-catering classification changes taking effect 1 April 2027
findings.detail: The paper says the Welsh Government consultation considered a modest reduction to the 182-day threshold and extended exemptions, and that these changes would reduce the tax base and the premium income collected. The outcome and the number of affected properties are not yet known, so the base has not been adjusted. The paper also expects some self-catering units to move back to NDR once the Valuation Office clears its appeals backlog.
findings.matters: Other councils with self-catering stock face the same pending reclassification, and the base figure here excludes a reduction the paper itself expects.
findings.figures: 182-day letting threshold; 1 April 2027 effective date; 252 days available to be let
findings.quote: it has not been possible to adjust the Council Tax Base

findings.matters: The arrears balance is the source the paper names for covering any current-year collection shortfall, so its growth bears directly on the budget's exposure.

findings.matters: A higher collection assumption is being set while the in-year rate is reported as falling, so the budget depends more on arrears recovery than on current-year collection.

findings.matters: A future convergence policy could change the rent trajectory that long-term HRA business plans assume, so finance directors may want to track it.
findings.quote: underway into rent convergence, with a report now expected later in the Autumn.

findings.matters: The return deadline and published compliance report create a dated assurance obligation that finance and housing teams must evidence, and that peers can compare against.

findings.headline: Pembrokeshire projects its capital financing costs at 3.65% of net revenue stream for 2026-27, against a 5.30% cap
findings.detail: The council reports that at Quarter 2 the ratio of capital financing costs to net revenue stream is projected at 3.65% for 2026-27, within the 5.30% cap recommended to be maintained for 2026-27. The paper also states that borrowing costs remain significantly higher than assumed when many schemes were developed.
findings.matters: The affordability ratio against a fixed cap is the test a finance director uses to judge whether further borrowing can be supported, and the paper flags that schemes were developed on lower cost assumptions.

It also says it will minimise interest costs on loans taken in the year.
findings.matters: A revised borrowing-rate assumption is a direct signal to finance directors comparing budgeted and expected financing costs, and to lenders assessing the council's expected cost of new funding.

findings.detail: The paper says the current direction applies until 31 March 2030, and that capital receipts can be used to fund revenue expenditure needed to transform services and generate ongoing revenue savings. This includes redundancy costs, which the council intends to capitalise where possible.
findings.matters: Capitalising redundancy and transformation costs moves cost out of the revenue budget, which is a route other councils use to fund savings, and it is limited by the amount of capital receipts available.
findings.figures: £8.256m (capital receipts earmarked from 2026-27)
findings.quote: A Capitalisation Direction, issued by Welsh Government, enables Capital Receipts to be used to fund revenue expenditure required to transform and generate ongoing revenue savings.

findings.paper_title: Outline Draft County Council Budget 2027-2028 and Outline Draft Medium Term Financial Plan (MTFP) 2027-2028 to 2029-2030
findings.headline: Budget savings identified for 2027-28 total £21.8m, with 41.7% rated Red 1, Red 2 or Deep Red
findings.detail: Directorates have identified £21.8m of savings, RAG-rated by impact on the public. The report states that 41.7% of these are very challenging with significant impact, at risk of statutory failings, or very significant impact, and that implementation will be challenging.
findings.matters: A high share of savings in the most severe RAG bands signals delivery risk that lenders and peer finance officers will want to track against eventual outturn.
findings.figures: £21.8m total savings; 41.7% in Red 1, Red 2 and Deep Red; Social Care & Housing £13.2m
findings.quote: As can be seen in the table above 41.7% of the budget savings identified have been categorised as very challenging with significant impact on service delivery or at risk of statutory failings and/or very significant impact

findings.paper_title: Outline Draft County Council Budget 2027-2028 and Outline Draft Medium Term Financial Plan (MTFP) 2027-2028 to 2029-2030
findings.headline: Pembrokeshire projects a 2027-28 funding gap of £18.7m, rising to £50.0m across the MTFP 2027-28 to 2029-30 (most likely scenario)
findings.detail: The report sets the projected funding gap at £18.7m for 2027-28 and £50.0m over the three-year MTFP, described as the increase in net expenditure needed to continue delivering current services. It notes the gap will change as settlement figures are confirmed.
findings.matters: A finance director here or at a peer council can compare the size of the gap, and the stated bridging options, against their own MTFP position.
findings.quote: The projected funding gap for 2027-28 is currently £18.7m and over the MTFP 2027-28 to 2029-30 is £50.0m (most likely scenario)

findings.headline: 490-home housing programme 2024-32 dependent on continued second homes premium funding
findings.detail: The HRA business plan includes 490 homes planned, under construction, or built between 2024-25 and 2031-32 through both direct council build and grant support to partners (Solva CLT, Homebuy scheme). The council allocated £5.5m from the premium reserve in 2025-26 for housing development. Future programme delivery is explicitly dependent on ongoing availability of grant support from second homes premium revenue.
findings.matters: Housing delivery is a stated council priority; a lender assesses whether capital plans are executable. The dependence on discretionary premium revenue which has already been cut (150% to 125%) creates execution risk for the housing programme.
findings.figures: 490 homes planned 2024-25 to 2031-32; £5.5 million allocated 2025-2026 from second homes premium reserve
findings.quote: Future developments are dependent on availability of grant support (including second homes premium) and in total, between 2024-25 through to 2031-32 a total of 490 homes are either planned, under construction or built.

findings.headline: Holiday let numbers fell 30% after Valuation Office backlog cleared in October 2024; further reclassifications likely as backlog remains
findings.detail: The 182-day letting threshold for holiday let exemption changed in April 2023, but administrative backlog at the Valuation Office prevented reclassification until October 2024, when holiday let numbers suddenly fell 30%. The Valuation Office backlog for reviews and appeals remains, and Welsh Government is consulting on whether to reduce the threshold further, creating ongoing uncertainty in the council's tax base.
findings.matters: Tax base volatility makes revenue forecasting unreliable; properties reclassifying between non-domestic rates and council tax affect which properties are subject to premiums, creating further uncertainty in discretionary premium income that the council now depends on for core services.
findings.figures: 30% fall in holiday lets after October 2024; backlog partially cleared; some properties transferred from NDR (non-domestic rates) to council tax as second homes
findings.quote: Although the 182-day actual letting threshold change was made on 1 April 2023, the number of holiday lets remained largely unchanged until October 2024 after which the total number of holiday lets fell by 30%.

findings.headline: Solva Community Land Trust affordable housing project has experienced significant delays; 18 homes approved December 2019 not yet delivered as of March 2026
findings.detail: The project was approved in principle December 2019 with a target completion date of summer 2021. Grant funding was formally committed from the second homes premium reserve in October 2020. As of March 2026 report, the project remains undelivered with significant delays; the council is restructuring the arrangement and the developer awaits planning permission for additional units.
findings.matters: Capital delivery delays signal execution risk in the council's housing programme; this project relied on discretionary premium funding that is now at risk given premium rate reductions. A lender assesses whether the council can deliver promised housing stock.
findings.figures: 18 affordable houses; approved December 2019; grant committed 5 October 2020; March 2026 status report
findings.quote: On 5 October 2020 Cabinet authorised the award of a grant from the Second Homes Council Tax fund to Ateb Housing Association (working alongside Solva Community Land Trust) 18 new affordable houses.  Since then there have been significant delays.

findings.headline: £33.5m annually from second homes and empty homes premiums allocated to general fund budget since 2024-25, planned to continue through medium term
findings.detail: The council has structured its budget to allocate premium revenue directly to core services: homelessness (£2.05m), schools (£4.71m), public realm maintenance (£1.15m), youth services (£0.9m). This arrangement is planned to continue through 2027-28 and the medium term, creating structural dependence on discretionary revenue streams.
findings.matters: This creates material revenue risk: if premium rates fall further or if second homes/empty homes properties decline in number, core service budgets face pressure. A lender needs to understand whether the general fund budget is sustainable if premium income reduces.
findings.figures: £33.5m allocated since 2024-25; homelessness £2,050k; schools £4,708k; public realm £1,150k
findings.quote: Since 2024-25 £33.5m has been allocated to the general fund budget in respect of elements of the budget relating to affordable housing and enhancing the sustainability of local communities and it is proposed that this arrangement will continue in 2027-28 and over the medium term.

findings.headline: Second homes council tax premium reduced from 150% to 125% in 2026-27, with tourism industry impact cited as main reason
findings.detail: The council deliberately reduced the premium rate in October 2025, marking the second rate change in three years (100% in 2022-23, 200% in 2024-25, now 125%). The reduction explicitly acknowledges tourism industry concerns as the primary driver of the policy shift, showing the council is balancing revenue objectives against economic pressure.
findings.matters: A lender needs to assess whether the council's revenue forecasts account for lower premium yield; a peer council wants to understand how to navigate competing policy priorities (housing affordability vs. economic resilience).
findings.quote: It is clear from Council's October 2025 minutes when it decided to reduce the second home council tax premium rate from 150% to 125%, that one of the main reasons was the potential impact on the tourism industry.

findings.paper_title: Council - Council Tax Premium for Long-Term Empty Properties
findings.headline: £22.3m projected funding gap for 2027-28; a 25% change to long-term empty property premium rate would impact the gap by only circa £0.2m
findings.detail: The Director of Resources projects a £22.3m funding gap for 2027-28. Even substantial changes to the long-term empty property premium rate would yield only marginal budget relief (£0.2m per 25% change), illustrating that this revenue source has limited capacity to address the underlying structural deficit.
findings.matters: Demonstrates the scale of the council's budget challenge and that discretionary revenues are insufficient to bridge it; raises questions about the sustainability of a budget model that uses these revenues to fund core services.
findings.figures: £22.3m funding gap (2027-28). A 25% decrease in premium would increase the gap by circa £0.2m; a 25% increase would reduce it by circa £0.2m.
findings.quote: The projected funding gap for 20 27-28 is currently £2 2.3m, albeit it is hoped that this will reduce over the coming months...a 25% decrease in the premium would increase the funding gap for 2027 -28 by circa. £0.2m, with a 25% increase in the premium reducing the funding gap for 2027-28 by circa £0.2m.

findings.paper_title: Council - Council Tax Premium for Long-Term Empty Properties
findings.headline: Council uses long-term empty property premium income to fund homelessness and schools; second homes premium has been cut twice in recent years (£2.3m + £1.3m cumulative impact), triggering the flagged budget risk
findings.detail: The long-term empty property premium (£1.4m annually) and second homes premium fund essential services: homelessness support (£2.05m), schools (£4.7m), and housing standards. The Director of Resources explicitly flagged a "potential future risk" if premium income dropped or council discretion changed. This risk has already materialized twice: second homes premium fell from 200% to 150% (2025-26, creating £2.3m pressure) then to 125% (2026-27, creating £1.3m pressure), showing a pattern of cutting discretionary revenues under budget pressure.
findings.matters: Shows essential services depend on council's own policy decisions about discretionary revenues; precedent indicates the council cuts premiums when facing financial pressure, creating structural budget vulnerability.
findings.figures: £1,413k raised from long-term empty property premium (2025-26). Second homes premium reductions created £2.3m and £1.3m additional pressures in successive years.
findings.quote: This risk was realised with the Council decision to reduce the Second Homes Council Tax Premium from 200% to 150% for 2025 -26 creating an additional £2.3m pressure for the 2025 -26 Budget and was realised again with the Council decision to reduce the premium to 125% for 2026 -27 creating an additional £1.3m pressure on the 2026 -27 Budget.

findings.paper_title: Council - Council Tax Premium for Long-Term Empty Properties
findings.headline: Long-term empty properties subject to 300% premium fell 4% to 448 from 467, indicating policy is achieving its aim of bringing properties back into use
findings.detail: The number of properties attracting the premium has declined since its introduction, suggesting the levy is successfully incentivizing owners to re-occupy dwellings. However, this also means the tax base is gradually shrinking: as the policy succeeds, the revenue available to fund the services it supports will decline.
findings.matters: Finance directors need visibility of whether discretionary revenue streams are sustainable; a declining tax base creates future pressure.
findings.figures: 467 properties in 2025; 448 in 2026. Overall empty properties increased from 2,775 to 2,915.
findings.quote: The number of properties subject to the long -term empty property premium has reduced from 467 in 2025 to 448 in 2026, suggesting that the premium may be contributing towards bringing some long -term empty properties back into use.

findings.headline: Auditor identified no material uncertainties relating to going concern
findings.detail: The auditor concluded that no material uncertainties exist that would cast significant doubt on the council's ability to continue as a going concern for at least 12 months from the date accounts are authorised for issue. This conclusion was reached despite the control and capacity issues identified.
findings.matters: Going concern is fundamental to credit risk assessment. A clear going concern conclusion provides assurance the council is not facing immediate operational or financial threats, though it does not address the control quality failures identified.
findings.figures: No figures
findings.quote: I have not identified any material uncertainties relating to events or conditions that, individually or collectively, may cast significant doubt on Pembrokeshire County Council's ability to continue as a going concern.

findings.headline: Unqualified audit opinion issued on 2024-25 accounts with no uncorrected misstatements remaining
findings.detail: The auditor issued an unqualified opinion on the 2024-25 financial statements, confirming they give a true and fair view and were properly prepared. No uncorrected misstatements remained in the final accounts following management's correction of errors identified during the audit process.
findings.matters: An unqualified opinion provides assurance on accounts reliability. However, this conclusion was reached only after extensive audit work to identify and have corrected numerous material errors, indicating the pre-audit draft quality was poor despite the ultimate unqualified opinion.
findings.figures: No figures
findings.quote: We intend to issue an unqualified opinion on the accounts. There are no uncorrected misstatements in the accounts.

findings.headline: Council planning to audit two financial years within 10-month window to return to statutory deadlines
findings.detail: To recover from current delays, the council aims to submit the 2025-26 draft accounts by 23 November 2026 (audit completion by 31 March 2027) and the 2026-27 draft accounts by 30 June 2027 (audit completion by 30 September 2027). The auditor describes this as a challenging timetable requiring high-quality statements and comprehensive working papers available at the start of each audit.
findings.matters: This ambitious catch-up schedule signals the seriousness of the delay problem but creates concentration risk. Failure to meet these dates would indicate persistent control problems; success would demonstrate whether capacity improvements are working.
findings.figures: 23 November 2026 (2025-26 draft); 31 March 2027 (2025-26 audit); 30 June 2027 (2026-27 draft); 30 September 2027 (2026-27 audit)
findings.quote: This is a challenging timetable, as two audit cycles will need to be completed within 10 months. We will continue to work with officers to support delivery within these timescales, but this will require officers to prepare high-quality statements within agreed timeframes supported by comprehensive and accurate working papers.

findings.headline: Council recruited technical accountant and appointed qualified valuer by 31 October 2026 to rebuild asset accounting capacity
findings.detail: In response to identified capacity gaps, the council recruited a Technical Accountant to support complex capital accounting, appointed a qualified valuer in the property function, and completed a property service team restructure. These actions are intended to strengthen quality assurance and capacity for asset accounting, with implementation targeted for 31 October 2026.
findings.matters: Whether these staffing actions prove sufficient and are implemented timely will determine whether control failures recur. Lenders and other councils assess the credibility of remedial actions and the council's commitment to sustainable solutions.
findings.figures: Implementation date 31 October 2026
findings.quote: In response, the Council has strengthened its arrangements through the recruitment of a Technical Accountant to support the preparation and review of the more complex capital accounting requirements. In addition, the Property Service has appointed a qualified valuer and completed a team restructure which has increased capacity.

findings.headline: Council identified lack of capacity and specialist knowledge in technical accounting and property functions as root cause
findings.detail: The auditor identified significant and interrelated asset accounting issues; the council's subsequent review attributed the root cause to lack of capacity and specialist knowledge within technical accounting and property functions. This capacity constraint limited the council's ability to quality assure information and valuations provided by external consultants.
findings.matters: Identifying root causes shows management is addressing the real problem, but also signals continued risk if capacity and expertise are not rapidly restored. Finance directors and lenders assess whether staffing solutions are sufficient to prevent recurrence.
findings.figures: No figures
findings.quote: The Council has undertaken a thorough review of the issues encountered during the preparation and audit of the 2024-25 Statement of Accounts and has identified the primary root causes as a lack of capacity and specialist knowledge within both the technical accounting and property functions.

findings.headline: IFRS16 Leases implementation produced methodology and calculation errors requiring £2.1m correction
findings.detail: Implementation of the new IFRS16 Leases accounting standard, effective from 1 April 2024, generated errors in the identification and calculation of lease arrangements. The audit identified errors in methodology and calculations, resulting in a net £2.13m adjustment to right of use assets and a £1.4m formula error in lessor receipts disclosure.
findings.matters: IFRS16 materially affects both assets and liabilities on the balance sheet and creates new disclosure requirements about future lease commitments. Implementation errors indicate the council struggled with a complex new standard, relevant to other councils facing similar compliance challenges.
findings.figures: £2,131,000 (right of use asset adjustment); £1,400,000 (lessor receipts formula error)
findings.quote: Significant additional work was required during the audit to ensure that all potential lease arrangements had been appropriately considered and that working papers were complete and producing accurate figures as we identified errors in the methodology and calculations used.

findings.headline: Property, plant and equipment corrected by £24.1m for asset ownership and revaluation basis errors
findings.detail: The audit identified significant errors in the council's accounting for fixed assets, requiring corrections of £6.16m relating to assets not owned or controlled by the council and assets not previously recognised, plus £17.96m in net revaluation basis adjustments. These errors indicate control failures in asset identification, classification and valuation processes.
findings.matters: Large corrections to asset values are material to the balance sheet, affect key financial ratios used in borrowing covenants, and indicate weak controls in critical accounting areas. Lenders may question the reliability of reported asset values and any security interests in those assets.
findings.figures: £6,160,000 (ownership/recognition adjustment); £17,961,000 (net revaluation basis decrease)
findings.quote: A series of assets included in the draft accounts were not owned or controlled by the Council. Additionally, assets were identified which had not been previously recognised by the Council... A series of amendments have been made to the revaluation basis of assets, which has resulted in an overall net decrease in the revaluation figure of £17,961,000.

findings.headline: Accounts submission delayed 4+ months beyond statutory deadline, audit certification expected 12 months late
findings.detail: The council submitted its 2024-25 accounts for audit on 12 November 2025, over four months after the statutory deadline of 30 June 2025. Audit certification is expected 16 October 2026, approximately 12 months after the statutory deadline of 31 October 2025. This timeline reflects significant issues with account preparation quality and capacity.
findings.matters: Finance directors and lenders depend on timely audited accounts to assess financial position and statutory compliance. Delays of this magnitude indicate control weaknesses and capacity constraints that could affect ongoing financial management and borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: Submission 12 November 2025 (vs 30 June 2025 deadline); expected certification 16 October 2026 (vs 31 October 2025 deadline)
findings.quote: The accounts were submitted to us for audit on 12 November 2025, which was after the statutory deadline of 30 June 2025. We are aiming to certify your accounts on 16 October 2026. This is later than the statutory deadline of 31 October 2025.

findings.headline: Auditor General's audit opinion found no matters of concern; all governance statements confirmed; internal audit found no issues
findings.detail: The external auditor's opinion is unqualified. All eight governance confirmations were marked as met. Internal audit examined ten control objectives and reported no issues identified across any of them.
findings.matters: A finance director needs confirmation that governance and financial controls are functioning properly and that reported statements are reliable, even where underlying financial position raises concerns
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: no matters have come to my attention giving cause for concern that in any material respect, the information reported in this Annual Return: has not been prepared in accordance with proper practices

findings.headline: Fixed and long-term assets decreased by £539,283 (14.7%) to £3,118,002
findings.detail: The Harbour Authority's asset base fell from £3,657,285 to £3,118,002 in the year. For a body managing harbour infrastructure, this material reduction requires explanation—whether through asset disposal, revaluation, depreciation, or other means—as these assets are core to its function.
findings.matters: A material change in the asset base of a public harbours authority would alert a finance director to potential service contraction, asset disposal decisions, or balance sheet corrections with implications for the authority's capability
findings.quote: Total fixed assets and long-term assets 3,657,285 3,118,002

findings.headline: The Harbour Authority's balance sheet deficit increased by £61,801 to £443,262, financed entirely by creditors with no cash in hand
findings.detail: The Tenby & Lower Fishguard Harbours Authority shows liabilities exceeding assets by £443,262 at 31 March 2025, compared to a deficit of £381,461 at 31 March 2024. With zero cash and only £12,373 of debtors, the authority's position is entirely dependent on creditor funding. Creditors owed increased from £381,461 to £455,635, representing 187% of annual receipts.
findings.matters: A joint committee managing public infrastructure with a growing deficit and no cash reserves indicates either an unsustainable operational model or an increasing funding requirement that the parent council must sustain
findings.quote: Balances carried forward (381,461) (443,262) Total balances should equal line 7 above: Enter the total of (8+9-10)

findings.headline: Council recommends keeping premium rates unchanged from 2025-26 despite declining political support
findings.detail: Pembrokeshire Cabinet recommended on 5 October 2026 that council tax premium rates remain unchanged from 2025-26 for 2027-28. This decision was made despite consultation showing declining support for the premiums and despite a Notice of Motion asking for changes to discretionary policies on second home discounts.
findings.matters: Confirms the council's intent to maintain current revenue assumptions for budget planning; absence of rate increase despite declining support suggests revenue maintenance is prioritised over political accommodation.
findings.figures: 125% second homes premium maintained from 2025-26
findings.quote: The proposal assessed is the recommended by Cabinet at its 5 October meeting is that the premiums and the use of funding generated by them is unchanged from 2025-26.

findings.headline: Second homes and holiday lets grew by only 10 properties over 2025-26, suggesting premium has stabilised the market
findings.detail: The combined total of second homes and NDR self-catering properties reached 6,268 at end of 2025-26, an increase of only 10 from the prior year. The council's assessment is that the 125% premium is sufficient to prevent further growth, implying the policy is achieving its constraint objective while revenue remains stable.
findings.matters: Shows the £9m revenue is being raised from a relatively stable property base; further policy tightening is unlikely to yield additional revenue through property reduction, but the base appears locked in.
findings.figures: 10 additional properties; 6,268 total combined second homes and NDR holiday lets
findings.quote: Over 2025-26 the combined number of second homes and NDR holiday lets is little changed with an increase of 10 properties to 6,268 over a year.

findings.headline: Consultation support for second homes premium has declined, with 53% of respondents now opposing any premium
findings.detail: In the 2026 consultation, 53% of respondents did not want a second home premium at all, up from 43% in 2023. Among second home owners themselves, only 2% support the current 125% rate. Very few respondents support premiums above 100%. This declining support for the policy creates political risk to a revenue stream the council is relying on for budget closure.
findings.matters: Political risk to the revenue assumption: if opposition continues to grow, the council may face pressure to reduce or eliminate premiums, eroding expected income.
findings.figures: 53% no premium (2026) vs 43% (2023); 2% of second home owners prefer current 125% rate; 11% of all respondents support 100% or higher
findings.quote: The percentage of second home-owners who do not want a premium has increased over the past four years.

findings.headline: Ministerial direction constrains £5.5m of premium revenue for affordable housing programme
findings.detail: Welsh Government has issued a ministerial direction requiring that £5.5m of funding raised from council tax premiums must be allocated to the council's HRA affordable housing programme. This is a statutory constraint on deployment of this revenue source.
findings.matters: Reduces flexibility in use of a discretionary revenue source; the council cannot redirect this portion to other budget pressures.
findings.quote: A ministerial direction has been agreed which will allow £5.5m of funding raised by the premiums to be used to support the Council's HRA affordable housing programme.

findings.headline: Council tax premiums are supporting closure of 2027-28 budget funding gap
findings.detail: Pembrokeshire is relying on £9m annual revenue from second homes and empty homes premiums to help close its anticipated funding gap for 2027-28. The council has maintained these premiums rather than reducing or eliminating them, confirming this revenue in its budget assumptions. The second homes premium is currently set at 125%, generating substantial revenue directed to affordable housing and community programmes.
findings.matters: Shows a council's budget plan depends on maintaining discretionary revenue sources at current levels; change to political tolerance or policy effectiveness could threaten this income.
findings.figures: £9m each year; 92% of funding directed to council budget elements relating to affordable housing and community sustainability
findings.quote: Should a premium continue to be set and (as currently) majority of funding is directed to the Council's budget, this will support closing the anticipated funding gap for 2027-28

findings.paper_title: Council - Council Tax Premium for Second Homes
findings.headline: Pembrokeshire's high proportion of second homes reduces Welsh Government funding allocation because it is based on population statistics
findings.detail: Welsh Government distributes funding based on Standard Spending Assessment and indicator-based assessment, which are predominantly population-based. Because Pembrokeshire has 4,559 second homes (with concentrations over 20% in coastal communities), the resident population count is artificially depressed, reducing the council's funding allocation below what it would receive if these were primary residences.
findings.matters: This creates a permanent structural funding disadvantage that cannot be solved through operational management. The second homes premium is a partial compensatory mechanism, but it is discretionary and already under pressure.
findings.figures: 4,559 second homes total (Aug 2026), up from 4,483; over 20% of dwellings in coastal communities are second homes
findings.quote: The significant number of second homes and long-term empty properties prevents the substantive population statistics in Pembrokeshire being as high as they would be without them, this results in the Authority receiving less funding through the service requirements distribution than would be expected should these properties be standard homes with Pembrokeshire living families.

findings.paper_title: Council - Council Tax Premium for Second Homes
findings.headline: Welsh Government policy changes on self-catering classification are shifting properties between Council Tax and non-domestic rates, creating uncertainty in the revenue base
findings.detail: From April 2023, reclassification of self-catering accommodation has moved properties between the second homes premium base and non-domestic rates. In Q1 2026-27 alone, 44 properties moved from NDR to Council Tax and 38 moved back, with the Valuation Office experiencing a backlog of determinations and ratepayers appealing decisions. This makes it difficult to assess whether premium changes are having intended policy effects.
findings.matters: When a significant portion of the revenue base is in flux due to external policy changes and an appeals backlog, councils cannot reliably project income or assess policy effectiveness.
findings.figures: 44 properties moved to Council Tax in Q1 2026-27; 38 moved back to NDR; self-catering units 1,700 (Oct 2025) to 1,829 (Aug 2026)
findings.quote: As these policy changes occurred alongside adjustments to the premium levels, it is difficult to isolate and assess the direct impact of the premium itself on property owner behaviour, housing availability, or the extent to which the intended policy objectives have been achieved.

findings.paper_title: Council - Council Tax Premium for Second Homes
findings.headline: Premium reductions from 200% to 150% to 125% created £2.3m and £1.3m budget pressures; further reductions would realize the same risk a third time
findings.detail: The council reduced the premium from 200% to 150% for 2025-26, creating £2.3m additional pressure. It then reduced to 125% for 2026-27, creating £1.3m further pressure. The Director of Resources explicitly identifies this pattern as a 'realized risk' and warns that another reduction would realize it again.
findings.matters: The pattern shows a council facing structural budget pressures, initially offsetting them via premium increases, then choosing to reduce the premium at fiscal cost. This signals both budget stress and political pressure against the tax.
findings.figures: £2.3m pressure 2025-26; £1.3m pressure 2026-27
findings.quote: This risk was realised with the Council decision to reduce the Second Homes Council Tax Premium from 200% to 150% for 2025-26 creating an additional £2.3m pressure for the 2025-26 Budget and was realised again with the Council decision to reduce the premium to 125% for 2026-27 creating an additional £1.3m pressure on the 2026-27 Budget. This risk would be realised for a third time should a decision be made to reduce the second homes Council Tax premium % for 2027-28.

findings.paper_title: Council - Council Tax Premium for Second Homes
findings.headline: 92% of second homes Council Tax premium income funds core budget functions; a 25% premium change moves the budget needle by £1.6m
findings.detail: The council allocates 92% of second homes premium income to support general budget pressures including homelessness, schools, and public realm maintenance, rather than ring-fencing it for housing. With a projected funding gap of £22.3m for 2027-28, a 25% reduction in premium would increase that gap by circa £1.4m, while a 25% increase would reduce it by circa £1.4m.
findings.matters: A council funding core services via discretionary premium income faces structural vulnerability if the premium is reduced, policy changes, or the tax base erodes.
findings.figures: 92% allocation to budget; £1.6m per 25% premium change; £22.3m projected funding gap 2027-28; homelessness allocation £2,050k
findings.quote: As 92% of the second homes Council Tax premium income is currently used to fund elements of the Council's budget relating to affordable housing and enhancing the sustainability of local communities, any increase in premium raised will reduce the budget pressure in 2027-28, whilst a reduction in premium level will increase the budget pressure for 2027-28.

findings.paper_title: Pembrokeshire County Council - Annual Audit Summary 2025
findings.headline: West Wales region continuing to experience high levels of delayed hospital discharges affecting emergency care capacity
findings.detail: A multi-council performance audit review identified ongoing challenges in supporting timely discharge from hospital across Pembrokeshire, Carmarthenshire, Ceredigion and Hywel Dda Health Board. Audit Wales issued 15 recommendations on capacity, discharge planning, information sharing, policy development and scrutiny arrangements to support regional improvement.
findings.matters: Delayed hospital discharge typically reflects adult social care capacity constraints; this can drive future service cost pressures and demand volatility, affecting council financial planning and resilience.
findings.figures: 15 recommendations across four partner organisations; 4-council regional review
findings.quote: High levels of delayed discharges continue to impact urgent and emergency care services.

findings.paper_title: Pembrokeshire County Council - Annual Audit Summary 2025
findings.headline: Council has significantly strengthened corporate risk management arrangements in recent years
findings.detail: Audit Wales found the council operates within an up-to-date risk management framework supported by a positive risk management culture. Four recommendations were made for further enhancement in risk appetite and tolerance, escalation and de-escalation criteria, and risk reporting.
findings.matters: Robust risk management is foundational to council financial resilience; strong governance frameworks support a lender's confidence in the council's ability to navigate financial pressures.
findings.figures: Four recommendations identified for further enhancement
findings.quote: Audit Wales found that the Council has significantly strengthened its risk management arrangements in recent years and now operates within an up-to-date framework supported by a positive risk management culture.

findings.paper_title: Pembrokeshire County Council - Annual Audit Summary 2025
findings.headline: Audit identified improvements needed in capital accounting processes before final sign-off
findings.detail: Audit Wales identified issues in capital transactions and balances that were corrected before final accounts approval. Recommendations were made to strengthen capital accounting processes and improve the timeliness of future financial statements.
findings.matters: Capital is typically material on local authority balance sheets; control weaknesses in capital accounting raise questions about the strength of underlying accounting control frameworks.
findings.figures: Specific amounts not disclosed; issues corrected before approval
findings.quote: Recommendations have been made to strengthen capital accounting processes and improve the timeliness of future financial statements.

findings.paper_title: Pembrokeshire County Council - Annual Audit Summary 2025
findings.headline: Draft 2024-25 accounts delivered after statutory deadline but received unqualified audit opinion with no material misstatements
findings.detail: Audit Wales received the council's draft accounts on 12 November 2025, after the statutory deadline. Improvements were needed in capital accounting, but these were corrected. Subject to council approval, an unqualified opinion is intended, with audit completion scheduled for 16 October 2026.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence both in the reliability of financial statements and in the council's ability to meet financial governance timelines; late submission signals a process control issue.
findings.figures: Accounts delivered 12 November 2025, audit completion 16 October 2026
findings.quote: Audit Wales received the Council's draft accounts on 12 November 2025, after the statutory deadline. Whilst improvements were required in relation to capital transactions and balances, the accounts were found to be properly prepared and materially accurate, with no uncorrected misstatements.

findings.headline: Compressed timetable for 2025-26 and 2026-27 audits requires completion of two audit cycles within ten months; draft 2025-26 accounts due 23 November 2026
findings.detail: To recover from 2024-25 delays and meet statutory deadlines, the council must submit draft 2025-26 accounts by 23 November 2026 and receive audit completion by 31 March 2027 at latest. This allows preparation of 2026-27 accounts by the 30 June 2027 deadline. The auditor explicitly describes this as 'a challenging timetable' and notes success depends on consistent delivery of high-quality statements and working papers.
findings.matters: This signals whether the council has resolved the underlying capacity and process issues that caused 2024-25 problems. Success is uncertain—the auditor states the timetable is challenging. Failure to meet 2025-26 deadlines would trigger further delays, renewed governance concerns, and potential need to disclose financial control deficiencies.
findings.figures: 23 November 2026 draft submission target; 31 March 2027 audit completion target; two audit cycles in ten months
findings.quote: This is a challenging timetable, as two audit cycles will need to be completed within 10 months.

findings.headline: Supporting working papers inconsistent with accounts and difficult to follow; audit queries took significant time to resolve; significant additional audit costs incurred
findings.detail: The auditor paused fieldwork to allow officers time to resolve asset accounting issues. Finance team sickness contributed to delays in responding to audit queries, particularly on issues requiring external valuer or IFRS16 system supplier consultation. These quality and timeliness issues resulted in significant additional audit costs, which the auditor will discuss separately with the Director of Resources.
findings.matters: Working paper quality directly impacts audit efficiency and cost. Unbudgeted audit costs represent a call on council resources. More importantly, these operational issues indicate resource constraints or process gaps in the finance function that may affect financial control and the ability to deliver services.
findings.figures: Significant additional audit costs incurred (amount not specified); implementation date for improvements 30 June 2027
findings.quote: Supporting working papers were not always consistent with the accounts and were sometimes difficult to follow. Responses to audit queries took a significant amount of time, particularly where officers needed to consult with the external valuer and/or the external supplier of the IFRS16 system.

findings.headline: IFRS16 lease accounting standard implementation identified errors in external system methodology and calculations, requiring significant additional audit work
findings.detail: The council procured an external system and supplier to support IFRS16 Leases implementation from 1 April 2024. Significant additional audit work was needed because errors were found in the system's methodology and underlying calculations, requiring rework before lease arrangements could be correctly recognized in the accounts.
findings.matters: IFRS16 is a material accounting change across all councils. Implementation difficulties in year one often recur in future years. This signals Pembrokeshire may face ongoing lease accounting quality issues unless root causes are addressed, affecting future audit efficiency and financial statement reliability.
findings.figures: £2,131,000 Right of Use Asset balance adjustment; errors in system methodology and calculations identified
findings.quote: Significant additional work was required during the audit to ensure that all potential lease arrangements had been appropriately considered and that working papers were complete and producing accurate figures as we identified errors in the methodology and calculations used.

findings.headline: Property revaluation net decreased £17,961,000 due to incorrect asset classification and inappropriate valuation basis; opening PPE balances adjusted £6,160,000 for unowned or unrecognized assets
findings.detail: Large corrections were required to asset values. Revaluations were corrected downward by £17.96m after incorrect asset classification and valuation technique errors were identified. Separately, £6.16m of opening PPE balances required adjustment for assets not owned by the council or previously unrecognized. Capital commitments were also understated by £9.703m.
findings.matters: Corrections of this magnitude indicate either weak asset management systems or loss of control over the asset register. For a council managing a significant property portfolio, this signals governance gaps in asset accountability that may persist unless root causes are addressed.
findings.figures: £17,961,000 revaluation decrease; £6,160,000 opening PPE adjustment; £9,703,000 capital commitments understatement
findings.quote: A series of amendments have been made to the revaluation basis of assets, which has resulted in an overall net decrease in the revaluation figure of £17,961,000. These include amendments relating to the incorrect classification of asset additions resulting in incorrect valuation techniques being applied, and in other instances, the incorrect valuation basis being applied.

findings.headline: Accounts submitted 12 November 2025, five months after the 30 June statutory deadline; audit certification due 16 October 2026, eleven months after the 31 October statutory deadline
findings.detail: The council submitted accounts for audit significantly late and the auditor will certify nearly a year after the statutory deadline. The unqualified opinion is ultimately issued but the extended timeline reflects operational issues in account preparation and audit delivery that neither finance directors nor lenders would normally expect.
findings.matters: Timely financial reporting is fundamental to oversight and lender confidence. Extended delays of this scale signal either persistent capacity constraints or process failures in the finance function that may continue to affect future years and service delivery.
findings.figures: Submitted 12 November 2025 (deadline 30 June 2025); certification 16 October 2026 (deadline 31 October 2025)
findings.quote: The accounts were submitted to us for audit on 12 November 2025, which was after the statutory deadline of 30 June 2025. We are aiming to certify your accounts on 16 October 2026. This is later than the statutory deadline of 31 October 2025.

findings.detail: The Auditor General for Wales issued an unqualified opinion on the financial statements. The auditor concluded that the going concern basis is appropriate and has not identified any material uncertainties relating to events or conditions that may cast significant doubt on the Council's ability to continue operations for at least 12 months.
findings.matters: An unqualified audit opinion with no going concern issues is a baseline expectation, but material to a lender as confirmation that the auditor has identified no material misstatements or financial sustainability risks in the statements presented.

findings.detail: The Council's actuarial valuation shows the Dyfed Pension Fund surplus increased from £112m to £201m. This reflects revaluation of fund assets and update of actuarial assumptions at the latest valuation date (31 March 2022).
findings.matters: Pension position improvement is positive for long-term financial resilience and reduces future employer contribution volatility, though a lender would note that the valuation is based on 2022 asset positions and actuarial assumptions that may shift at the next triennial revaluation.

findings.matters: Capital expenditure reduction is relevant to a lender assessing delivery capability and asset investment trajectory, especially where a council is managing a large asset base or has committed infrastructure programmes.

findings.matters: HRA arrears trends signal tenant payment capacity stress and collection risk; for councils borrowing on their housing stock, arrears escalation at this pace reduces the revenue certainty on which rental income projections depend.

findings.matters: A lender assessing debt sustainability needs visible evidence of revenue collection management; this scale of arrears growth in one year indicates either temporary shock or collection performance deterioration that will affect cash flow and funding capacity.

findings.paper_title: 5.1 - Council Tax Premium for Second Homes
findings.headline: Council allocates 92% of discretionary second homes tax premium income to fund core services budget, against a £23.3m budget gap for 2027-28.
findings.detail: The council allocates the majority of the second homes premium to general fund services including homelessness (£2.05m), schools (£4.71m) and public realm maintenance. The premium thus funds elements of core services that otherwise would need to be covered by other revenue sources. The Director of Resources notes that a 25% change in the premium level would change the 2027-28 budget gap by approximately £1.4m.
findings.matters: Depending on discretionary, politically sensitive revenue to fund core services creates structural financial risk, particularly when budget pressures are large.

findings.paper_title: 5.1 - Council Tax Premium for Long-Term Empty Properties
findings.headline: Council experienced £3.6m budget pressures from prior reductions in second homes Council Tax premium and is managing £23.3m projected funding gap for 2027-28 partly through discretionary premium income
findings.detail: The Director of Resources reports that reductions to the second homes Council Tax premium—from 200% to 150% for 2025-26 (£2.3m pressure) and further to 125% for 2026-27 (£1.3m pressure)—created material budget pressures. The council uses premium income to fund £9.008m of general fund spending (2026-27), primarily on homelessness support (£2.05m) and schools (£4.71m). With a £23.3m projected funding gap for 2027-28, the cabinet recommends maintaining the long-term empty property premium at 300% partly to avoid a third budget pressure event. The Director explicitly flags reliance on discretionary premium income as a key budget risk.
findings.matters: The council is using discretionary Council Tax premium income to fund core services, and has already experienced two material budget hits when member decisions reduced those premiums. A lender needs to understand this structural vulnerability and whether the council has alternative funding strategies for the gap.
findings.figures: £23.3m projected funding gap 2027-28; £2.3m budget pressure 2025-26; £1.3m budget pressure 2026-27; £9.008m general fund allocation from premiums 2026-27; £2.05m homelessness allocation; £4.71m schools allocation
findings.quote: This risk was realised with the Council decision to reduce the Second Homes Council Tax Premium from 200% to 150% for 2025-26 creating an additional £2.3m pressure for the 2025-26 Budget and was realised again with the Council decision to reduce the premium to 125% for 2026-27 creating an additional £1.3m pressure on the 2026-27 Budget. This this risk would be realised for a third time should a decision be made to reduce the Council Tax premiums % for 2027-28 or to reduce its allocation to the Council's budget.

findings.headline: Council acquiring leasehold property from elected Cabinet Member at externally-valued market price of £85,000
findings.detail: Pembrokeshire County Council is proposing to acquire a three-bedroom leasehold maisonette in Hakin, Milford Haven through its Housing Revenue Account property buyback scheme. The property is currently held by an elected Councillor and Cabinet Member. To ensure transparency and independence given the related-party nature of the transaction, an external RICS valuer was specifically commissioned. The independent valuation, based on recent comparable sales in the locality, valued the property at £85,000. The council anticipates approximately £5,000 additional capital expenditure to bring the property into line with its housing standards. The property is held on a lease with approximately 88 years remaining.
findings.matters: Finance directors and lenders care about how councils manage related-party transactions and whether appropriate governance controls and independent valuations are applied to ensure fair market value and audit trail for acquisitions from elected members.

findings.quote: The majority of exemptions to premium at August 2026 relate to Class 1 (for sale) 121 properties (139 October 2025) and Class 6 (planning occupancy restriction) 600 properties (447 October 2025) due to self-catering properties transferring into Council Tax from NDR.
